title: The Ghost Commit
scenario: Participant Taylor modified README.md and immediately ran 'git commit -m "Update intro"', but Git printed the message below. Taylor is confused why the commit did not record the changes.
output_sim:
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   README.md

no changes added to commit (use "git add")
question: What critical step was missed before running git commit, and how should Taylor fix it?
options: README.md was not staged; run 'git add README.md' first.
The branch was locked; run 'git branch --unlock'.
Git needs an empty commit flag; run 'git commit --allow-empty'.
The file must be renamed to README.txt before committing.
explanation: In Git, changes in your working tree must first be staged (indexed) with 'git add' before they can be committed. Taylor needs to run 'git add README.md' (or 'git add .') to stage the modifications.
pro_tip: Think of staging as packing items into a shipping box ('git add'), and committing as taping the box shut with a label ('git commit').

title: The Merge Collision
scenario: Jordan ran 'git merge feature-login' into 'main'. Instead of completing cleanly, Git paused with the message below and inserted strange angle brackets inside auth.js.
output_sim:
Auto-merging auth.js
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in auth.js
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
question: What happened, and what are the exact steps Jordan must take to finish the merge?
options: Both branches modified the same lines in auth.js. Jordan must open auth.js, choose the correct code, remove conflict markers, then run 'git add auth.js' and 'git commit'.
Git crashed. Jordan must delete the .git folder and run 'git init' again.
Jordan must immediately shut down their computer to cancel the merge.
The file auth.js is permanently corrupted and cannot be used.
explanation: A merge conflict happened because opposing edits occurred on the same lines. Jordan must open auth.js in an editor, decide which code to keep, delete the '<<<<<<<', '=======', and '>>>>>>>' markers, stage the file with 'git add auth.js', and commit.
pro_tip: VS Code and modern editors provide handy 'Accept Current', 'Accept Incoming', or 'Accept Both' clickable buttons right above the conflict markers!

title: The Detached Navigator
scenario: A student wanted to check an old commit and ran 'git checkout a1b2c3d'. Now their terminal prompt says 'HEAD detached at a1b2c3d'. They want to know what this means.
output_sim:
HEAD detached at a1b2c3d
nothing to commit, working tree clean
question: What does 'detached HEAD' mean, and how does the student safely return to their main branch?
options: HEAD points directly to a commit hash instead of a branch. Run 'git switch main' to return safely.
The repository has lost its internet connection; restart Wi-Fi.
All branches have been deleted from the hard drive.
The user's GitHub account has been logged out.
explanation: Detached HEAD means you are looking directly at a past commit snapshot rather than standing on a branch tip. Running 'git switch main' (or 'git checkout main') returns you to your active main branch without losing any work.
pro_tip: If you want to experiment starting from an old commit, create a new branch from it with 'git switch -c my-experiment'!

title: The Rejected Cloud Push
scenario: Samantha made a great commit locally and tried pushing to GitHub, but Git rejected the push with the output below.
output_sim:
To https://github.com/foss-mec/project.git
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/foss-mec/project.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do
hint: not have locally. This is usually caused by another repository pushing
hint: to the same ref. You may want to first integrate the remote changes
hint: (e.g., 'git pull ...') before pushing again.
question: Why did Git reject the push, and what is the proper fix?
options: A teammate pushed new commits to GitHub that Samantha does not have locally. Samantha must run 'git pull origin main' to merge them first, then push.
Samantha is not an administrator on GitHub; she must delete her repository.
Samantha must use 'git push --force' to overwrite her teammates' work.
The GitHub server is down for maintenance.
explanation: Git prevents you from accidentally overwriting commits that exist on the remote repository. Running 'git pull' fetches and merges the teammate's latest commits into your local branch so you can safely push.
pro_tip: Never run 'git push --force' on shared team branches like 'main', because it erases your teammates' commits from GitHub history!

title: The Regretted Edit
scenario: Alex accidentally made experimental changes in 'server.js' that broke the app. The file has NOT been staged with 'git add'. Alex wants to instantly throw away these uncommitted changes and return to the last commit.
output_sim:
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   server.js

no changes added to commit (use "git add")
question: Which modern command instantly reverts server.js back to the clean, committed version?
explanation: 'git restore <file>' discards unstaged changes in your working directory and restores the file exactly as it was in your last commit.
pro_tip: 'git restore' is safe and specific to the file you name. To restore all unstaged files in the folder, use 'git restore .'.

title: The Mysterious Modified Files
scenario: Alex just pulled a seat at the laptop after a quick break and forgot which files were edited before lunch. How can Alex quickly inspect which files have changed in the workspace?
output_sim:
On branch main
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.

Changes not staged for commit:
	modified:   index.html
	modified:   styles.css

Untracked files:
	notes.txt
question: Which command displays this exact overview of modified and untracked files?
explanation: 'git status' is your radar in Git. It reports current branch status, uncommitted changes, staged files, and untracked files.
pro_tip: Run 'git status' before and after every major command—it's the safest habit in version control.

scenario: The team noticed a bug introduced yesterday. Jordan wants to view the history of past commits, including who authored them, their timestamps, and the commit messages.
output_sim:

question: Which command allowed Jordan to inspect this chronological history of commits?
explanation: 'git log' displays the full commit history starting from the most recent commit back to the beginning of the repository.
pro_tip: Use 'git log --oneline --graph' to get a concise, beautiful tree visualization of your project's history.

title: The Missing Local Copy
scenario: A student finds an open-source practice project on GitHub at 'https://github.com/foss-mec/practice-repo.git' and wants to download a full local copy of the code and Git history onto their laptop.
output_sim:
Cloning into 'practice-repo'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 24, done.
remote: Counting objects: 100% (24/24), done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (18/18), done.
Receiving objects: 100% (24/24), 4.12 KiB | 4.12 MiB/s, done.
question: Which command downloads an existing GitHub repository onto your laptop?
explanation: 'git clone <URL>' downloads a complete duplicate of the remote repository, creates a folder, and sets up the 'origin' remote automatically.
pro_tip: Use 'git clone' only once per project. After that, use 'git pull' to fetch future updates.

title: The Feature Isolation Mission
scenario: During Day 2's collaborative demo, the facilitator instructs everyone to create a new branch named 'add-my-section' so they don't modify 'main' directly, and switch to it immediately in one command.
question: What is the recommended modern Git command to create and switch to a branch simultaneously?
explanation: 'git switch -c <branch-name>' creates and switches to the new branch in a single command. ('git checkout -b <branch-name>' also works in older Git versions).
pro_tip: Branches let you experiment safely without breaking working code on the 'main' branch.

title: The Emergency Interruption
scenario: Maya has half-written changes across 4 files on her feature branch. Her manager asks her to urgently switch to 'main' and pull a production fix. Running 'git switch main' gives an error because her working tree is dirty.
output_sim:
error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout:
	config.json
Please commit your changes or stash them before you switch branches.
Aborting
question: How can Maya safely shelve her uncommitted changes so she can switch branches immediately?
options: Run 'git stash' to save uncommitted changes onto a temporary stack, switch to main, and later run 'git stash pop'.
Delete config.json so Git doesn't complain.
Force switch with 'git switch -f main' and discard all her work.
Shut down the terminal and open a new project.
explanation: 'git stash' temporarily stashes away your dirty working state without creating a permanent commit. You can freely switch branches, and later reapply your stashed work with 'git stash pop'.
pro_tip: 'git stash' is one of the most beloved tools in Git for handling unexpected context switches!

title: The Accidental Secret Key
scenario: David added an API key file 'secrets.env' and ran 'git add secrets.env'. Before committing, David realizes this private key must NEVER be pushed to GitHub. How should David un-stage it?
output_sim:
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
	new file:   secrets.env
question: Which command removes secrets.env from the staging area without deleting the file from disk?
explanation: 'git restore --staged <file>' removes the file from the upcoming commit snapshot while leaving your local file completely intact on your hard drive.
pro_tip: Always add private keys, database passwords, and .env files to your '.gitignore' file so Git never tracks them!

title: The Upstream Link
scenario: A student made a commit on their new branch 'add-my-section'. When they tried running just 'git push', Git paused with the message below.
output_sim:
fatal: The current branch add-my-section has no upstream branch.
To push the current branch and set the remote as upstream, use

    git push --set-upstream origin add-my-section
question: What should the student do to publish this new branch to GitHub for the first time?
options: Delete the branch with 'git branch -D add-my-section' and try on main.
Turn off the Wi-Fi and push locally.
explanation: When pushing a brand new local branch for the first time, GitHub doesn't know about it yet. The '-u' (or '--set-upstream') flag tells Git to create a matching remote branch and link your local branch to it.
pro_tip: Once upstream is configured with '-u', all future pushes on that branch can be done with just 'git push'!
